stories.summary: While researching for an episode with Lant Pritchett, Amit landed on a strand of thinking that nation-states and city-governments have radically different origins. Nation-states evolved top-down and coercively — first priority was tax revenue and conscription for war, with little obligation in return. City-states evolved bottom-up — once people lived together beyond a certain size, there was an organic need for order, rule of law, and basic services. India inherited the larger coercive superstructure of the nation-state with no concept of a truly responsive bottom-up government.
stories.insight: The intellectual package you inherit shapes everything you can imagine. India centralised because it copied the British empire's coercive superstructure but lost the local-government training ground that produced its founding leaders — the package determined the limits of the state.

stories.topic: India's Founding Leaders Were Empowered Mayors First
stories.summary: Not so long ago, India had genuinely empowered mayors. C. Rajagopalachari was effectively mayor of Salem in 1917 as chairman of the municipal board. Jawaharlal Nehru held a similar position in Allahabad in 1923. Chittaranjan Das held it in Calcutta, then Subhas Chandra Bose. Sardar Patel was prominent in the Allahabad Municipal Council. Under the British Empire, local governments handled tasks the colonial government couldn't be bothered with — and it served as a training ground for these future leaders.
stories.insight: It's not true that India's founding leaders went straight from activist to politician. They knew governance, cared about it, understood public finance — and that crucible has been lost. India kept the colonial coercive superstructure but discarded the local training ground.

stories.summary: Many years ago, Lant Pritchett told Ajay that by some measures, the ratio of the richest place in Latin America to the poorest place in Africa is the same kind of number you get when you compare the richest place in India to the poorest place in India. India is that diverse and that heterogeneous internally.
stories.insight: The scale of internal heterogeneity makes India a first-order policy problem unlike any other country. A single design can't work — you can't run a 'Germany-style' homogeneous policy machine over a country whose internal range spans Latin America to Africa.

stories.summary: Drawing from Nilakantan RS's North vs South, Amit lays out two figures. Life expectancy: Kerala 75 (Argentina/Thailand), UP 64 (Liberia/Ethiopia/Haiti). Infant mortality (per thousand): Kerala 7 — better than the USA's 6 — Tamil Nadu 15, middling states 19-20, Madhya Pradesh 48. The same country contains both extremes.
stories.insight: The disparities aren't gaps you smooth out with a national policy — they're different countries operating under one flag. A central scheme calibrated to either pole will malfunction at the other.

stories.topic: Uttar Pradesh Equals France Plus Germany Plus Italy Plus Spain
stories.summary: From Karthik Muralidharan's data: the fifteen biggest Indian states would all be among the world's top 42 countries by population. Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined. Karthik further notes that the average Indian district is bigger than 85 countries in the world today — and those 85 countries would each demand democracy, but a district by definition cannot have democracy because everything is centralised above it.
stories.insight: We refer to UP as 'a state' and instinctively imagine one government can handle it. The arithmetic destroys that intuition. The governance unit is so far above any meaningful democratic scale that we have built sub-national tyrannies and called them democracy.

stories.topic: Susan Thomas, the Dog Bite, and Kerala Governance
stories.summary: Susan Thomas was bitten by a dog (she insists she was troubling the dog, so the dog was justified). The chain of surprises: (1) the family took her to a government clinic — in most of India, people like them would go private; (2) the clinic was open and the doctor was smart and competent; (3) the doctor asked the correct questions — is it a family dog, is it under observation? — and concluded that since the dog was fine, no rabies vaccination was needed, just antiseptic. Most Indian doctors, public or private, would have blasted nine injections of rabies vaccine.
stories.insight: A perfect concrete demonstration of why one-size-fits-all is wrong. Kerala's government health system actually works — most of India's doesn't. The right policy in Kerala (respect what they have) is the opposite of the right policy elsewhere (radically rebuild).

stories.summary: It comes as a surprise to most Indians that mosquitoes can actually be controlled — there is a great public health journey in mosquito control that India has given up on, fatalistically assuming people will just get malaria. But the characteristics of mosquitoes change every hundred or two hundred kilometres — they respond to natural selection, local weather, and the behaviour of their victims. So a mosquito control programme has to be local, varying by neighbourhood; only local people can solve their local mosquito problem.
stories.insight: Some problems are inherently local because the underlying biology is local. A central policy on mosquitoes can't work for the same reason a central policy on local accents can't work — the variance is the phenomenon.

stories.topic: Kerala Was Three Steps Ahead on COVID
stories.summary: Kerala had a head start on COVID because Malayali students returning from China brought the virus back. The state's health system was already running quarantines and isolation procedures while the Union government was doing nothing. Then the Union government started announcing nationwide lockdowns, and there was legitimate pushback from Kerala health: 'Hang on, we know what we're doing, we are probably three steps ahead of you. Don't tell us what to do.'
stories.insight: When a sub-national unit has built genuine state capacity, central instructions become a downgrade. Decentralisation isn't just a value statement; it's the operational truth that whoever has the local knowledge should drive.

stories.topic: Lancelot Pinto and the Paracetamol Approach
stories.summary: Amit recalls his episode with Dr Lancelot Pinto, who treated him through COVID twice. Pinto's funda was that many COVID deaths were happening from over-medication — patients would demand strong drugs, immune systems would overreact, and a week later they'd die not from COVID but from the medication. His approach: start with a paracetamol, and step it up only as needed. Amit took only paracetamol and cough syrup. Playing this way is courageous because 'playing by the book' is a safer move for a doctor — patients pop off from random things and blame the doctor.
stories.insight: Restraint in treatment requires institutional courage, because the asymmetric risk falls on the doctor: under-prescribe and you might be blamed; over-prescribe and the patient dies of the medicine but no one blames you. Good practice often runs against the doctor's own incentives.

stories.topic: The Catholic Church Lasted 1,650 Years on Subsidiarity
stories.summary: Economists love to claim the subsidiarity principle as their own, but it actually goes back to the Catholic Church — one of the world's most successful organisations. From around 300 AD to 1950, the Vatican controlled armies, joined international treaties, and outlasted most empires. Empires tended to crash partly because they centralised; the Catholic Church's design secret was the opposite — churches all over the world had their own autonomy, with the absolute minimum of central control.
stories.insight: Subsidiarity isn't an economist's abstraction — it's a survival pattern. Empires die because they centralise. Long-lived institutions distribute power down because that is what handles change without breaking.

stories.summary: After WWII, the Netherlands forgave Germany ('we know you invaded us a couple of times, but we let it go') and began buying German tanks. As a NATO member with maybe 20 tanks, the logistics tail of maintaining a tank battalion was sub-scale and silly. So they cut a deal: they'd pay for the tanks, but the tanks would be controlled by the German army on their behalf, with Dutch soldiers integrated into German units.
stories.insight: The European Union is a pragmatic, sensible approach to subsidiarity — don't draw lines on maps and then organise the state by lines on maps; for each problem, choose the right scale. Some things scale up (currency, defense), some scale down. Federalism done right is question-by-question, not territory-by-territory.

stories.topic: Vasant Dhar's Friend Baba Knows Everyone
stories.summary: Vasant Dhar's friend Baba claims to know everyone in the world. To prove it, they go to Trump Tower — the secretary lets him right in, and Donald hosts him for a meal. Then to the White House — Joe Biden spots Baba from the Oval Office, runs out (falling down a couple of times, his people picking him up), and greets him. Then to the Vatican on a festival day — Vasant gets separated in the crowd, and when the Pope appears on the balcony, Baba is up there with him. Someone next to Vasant taps him: 'Excuse me, who's that guy with Baba?'
stories.insight: A perfectly told joke for a federalism episode — celebrity, recognition, and the asymmetry of who's known to whom is the same problem as power and knowledge. Who is the central figure depends entirely on the frame you're standing in.

stories.summary: Linking to James C. Scott, Ajay notes that early states didn't compete for territory, they competed for people — that's what you wanted, people to oppress. From this worldview, the vast scale of migration in India is a celebration: people choose. Life in most urban slums is better than in most villages, and if it weren't, people wouldn't migrate. Rich Indians sitting in air-conditioned rooms have a 'luxury belief' that bemoans migration as some tragedy, when migration is in fact a market-based mechanism by which people sort themselves toward better governments.
stories.insight: Migration is not a problem to solve, it's a verdict the people are passing on the governments they've left. The governments people leave are the ones being voted against; what matters is people, not territory.

stories.topic: Power and Accountability Disconnected in Indian Cities
stories.summary: From Shruti Rajagopalan's observation: in any Indian city, governance is bad because power and accountability aren't linked. The people you (a city resident) have power over via municipal elections can't actually do much. The people who can actually do things — at the state level — aren't accountable to you because their vote bank is elsewhere. There's a fundamental mismatch built into the structure.
stories.insight: If the political feedback loop is broken at the city level, the city cannot improve regardless of how passionate the residents are. Decentralisation is not about preferences — it is about restoring the link between the lever you pull and the thing that moves.

stories.topic: Nehru's Trick of Amending the Constitution
stories.summary: Drawing from Shruti Rajagopalan's talk on India's constitutional amendments: Nehru started a tradition that whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional, he simply amended the constitution to make it constitutional — a cunning trick that immunised him from the courts. There's an early cartoon: a reader walks into the parliament bookshop and asks for a copy of the constitution. The bookshop replies: 'I'm sorry, we don't stock periodicals.'
stories.insight: When the foundational document becomes a periodical, the rule of law is replaced by the rule of the ruler. The constitution stops being a check on the executive and becomes its instrument.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Amit's recent deep-dive episode with the economist Lant Pritchett.
recommendations.reason: While researching for this episode, Amit landed on the city-state-vs-nation-state framing that opens this conversation. Pritchett's thinking is the seed of the decentralisation argument.

recommendations.item: CMIE Consumer Pyramids dx
recommendations.creator: Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE)
recommendations.context: A household survey dataset that divides India into about 100 homogeneous regions of about seven districts each.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's preferred way to see Indian heterogeneity numerically — incomes 5x apart between top and bottom regions, mobile-phone ownership 10-15x apart for women. The right tool for thinking past the national average.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on firm design.
recommendations.reason: The same intuition that drives this episode — in a homogeneous country one design propagates; in a heterogeneous country like India, firms (and governments) must build heterogeneity-coping information and incentives into themselves.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
recommendations.context: An episode with three thinkers on unconventional metrics of women's empowerment.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's favourite empowerment metrics — like who orders the groceries in the household. A useful counterweight to the standard income-and-literacy framing.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column from over a decade ago.
recommendations.reason: Argues that rising divorce rates in India should be celebrated, not bemoaned — they signal that more women are empowered with the agency and independence to walk away from bad marriages. A model of inverting a moral panic by inspecting what the metric actually measures.

recommendations.item: South vs North
recommendations.creator: Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: Nilakantan's book on the divergence between southern and northern India.
recommendations.reason: Source of the headline statistics in this episode — Kerala life expectancy 75 vs UP 64, Kerala IMR 7 vs Madhya Pradesh 48 — and the framing that India contains genuinely different countries by outcome.

recommendations.item: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive with Nilakantan RS on the same themes.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation behind the figures cited in this episode — the different policy responses needed for diabetes (Kerala's problem) versus malnutrition and stunting (the heartland's problem).

recommendations.item: Accelerating India's Development
recommendations.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Karthik Muralidharan's just-released book on Indian governance.
recommendations.reason: Source of the staggering scale comparisons — UP's size relative to Western Europe, the average Indian district being bigger than 85 countries, the 3% (India) vs 50% (China) of budget spent at local level.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (Episode 290, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier deep-dive with Karthik Muralidharan.
recommendations.reason: One of the long-form conversations where Karthik laid out the data on India's state size, scale, and governance challenges.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (Episode 375, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit's most recent episode with Karthik Muralidharan.
recommendations.reason: The third of four episodes — the source of the figures comparing India's 3% local-budget share to China's 50%, and the framing that China is 17x more decentralised than India.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the doctor Lancelot Pinto, who treated Amit through COVID twice.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Pinto laid out his 'don't over-medicate, start with paracetamol' philosophy and the courage required to play against the book in medicine.

recommendations.item: Brave New World
recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: A podcast hosted by Vasant Dhar, produced by Amit.
recommendations.reason: Amit produces the show; he plugs it before launching into the Baba-knows-everyone joke that Vasant once told him.

recommendations.item: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Pranay Kotasthane's newsletter post on horizontal vs vertical devolution in India.
recommendations.reason: The fable: two cats fighting over bread let a monkey mediate, who eats most of it while pretending to make the halves equal. Pranay's point — Indians worry too much about horizontal devolution (state-vs-state share) and not enough about vertical devolution (how much actually leaves the centre).

recommendations.item: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 17, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Amit's seven-year-old episode with Pranay Kotasthane.
recommendations.reason: The earlier conversation where Pranay made the same argument that Ajay echoes in this episode — that centrally sponsored schemes are an insidious form of central control over what is constitutionally state subjects.

recommendations.item: Shruti Rajagopalan on India's many constitutional amendments
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: A talk by Shruti Rajagopalan on the history of Indian constitutional amendments.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's anecdote that Nehru began the practice of amending the constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional — and the cartoon of the parliament bookshop refusing to stock 'periodicals.'

recommendations.item: Urban Governance in India (Episode 31, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: An older short episode with Shruti Rajagopalan on urban governance.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Shruti pointed out the fundamental mismatch in Indian cities — power and accountability aren't linked. The people residents have power over can't act; the people who can act aren't accountable to residents.

recommendations.item: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
recommendations.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.context: Hirschman's classic on the three responses to institutional decline.
recommendations.reason: American federalism leans heavily on 'exit' — if you don't like your city or state, move. India is used to either loyalty or a little voice. Migration is the under-emphasised exit lever, and tying tax revenue to where people live is what makes the exit lever bite.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: James C. Scott's work on early states.
recommendations.reason: Scott's frame that early states competed for people, not land — what you wanted was people to oppress. The lens that lets Ajay celebrate Indian migration as people moving away from worse governments toward better ones.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on India's population.
recommendations.reason: Ajay flags the demographic transition story he closed that earlier episode with — parts of India already in 'China territory' on births, making migration the only offset against demographic decline.

recommendations.item: The Power Broker
recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: Robert Caro's biography of Robert Moses, the man who shaped New York.
recommendations.reason: Re-recommended as essential reading on the philosophical clash between Robert Moses (top-down planner) and Jane Jacobs (organic, bottom-up city). The argument that runs through this entire episode.

recommendations.item: Triumph of the City
recommendations.creator: Edward Glaeser
recommendations.context: Edward Glaeser's book on cities as engines of human flourishing.
recommendations.reason: Re-recommended in the closing recos as a foundational text on why cities are the most important units in modern political economy.

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Jane Jacobs' masterpiece against modernist top-down urban planning.
recommendations.reason: Amit's headline reco. Cities evolve bottom-up; you need organic growth; cities are people more than buildings or highways. Jacobs is one of the great thinkers of the twentieth century, and everyone who lives in a city has skin in the game.

recommendations.item: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book on town planning
recommendations.creator: Bimal Patel
recommendations.context: An unreleased book by Bimal Patel, India's pre-eminent urban thinker on town planning.
recommendations.reason: Ajay reveals the secret that Bimal Patel is working on a book. When it comes out, run, not walk. Patel gets town planning in a way that essentially nobody else in India does.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the central argument applied throughout the episode — that economic growth follows from becoming a genuine republic with dispersion of power and check-and-balance, and that India's failures come from concentration of power.

core_ideas.explanation: Nation-states evolved coercively top-down — the priority was tax revenue and conscription for war, with no obligation to serve people in return. City-states evolved organically bottom-up — people lived together, exceeded a critical size, and developed an organic need for order, rule of law, and basic services. India's tragedy is that it inherited the coercive nation-state superstructure with no concept of bottom-up government. The mayoral training ground that produced India's founding leaders (Rajagopalachari, Nehru, Bose, Patel) under the British has been lost.
core_ideas.quote: We've never been allowed to evolve from the bottom up in modern times.

core_ideas.explanation: By any measure, India is internally as diverse as the gap between continents. Lant Pritchett's comparison: the ratio of richest-to-poorest within India is comparable to the ratio between richest Latin America and poorest Africa. Income across CMIE's 100 homogeneous regions varies 5x; women's mobile-phone ownership varies 10-15x; Kerala's life expectancy is Argentina's, UP's is Liberia's; Kerala's infant mortality is 7, Madhya Pradesh's is 48. A single national policy cannot fit such variance. The starting question for every policy must therefore be 'where' before 'what.'

Every function of government should be placed at the lowest level at which it can be done well — not the highest. Currency at the union; mosquito control at the village or city. Default to decentralisation; only centralise when decentralisation genuinely fails. Economists have stolen this from the Catholic Church, which lasted 1,650 years (300 AD to 1950) because it followed it: local churches with autonomy and minimum central control. Empires that centralised broke; the Vatican didn't.
core_ideas.quote: Above all we will be decentralized. We will be centralized for the few things where decentralization is really not feasible.

core_ideas.explanation: The European Union is not a country, by design. It's a pragmatic, sensible approach: don't draw lines on maps and define the state by lines on maps. Instead, for each question, choose the right scale. Currency at EU scale (the euro). National defence at EU scale (NATO). Personal law remains national, reflecting Catholic vs Protestant/secular preferences. Tank battalions for tiny armies fused into Germany's force structure. Everything finds its right level.

core_ideas.concept: The Concurrent List Is a Fantasy
core_ideas.explanation: India's constitution defines a union list, a state list, and a 'concurrent' list — the last imagined as a domain where wise CMs would negotiate with the PM in a collaborative spirit. In practice, the fine print specifies that if the union legislates on a concurrent subject, the union wins. So the concurrent list is the union's. The Planning Commission later went further, abusing tax sharing and centrally sponsored schemes to take over the state list too: 'I'll pay 65% if you do education my way.' This insidiously hijacks state resources and imposes a central design on what should be state subjects.
core_ideas.quote: There should be no centrally sponsored schemes, and the union should vacate the concurrent list. That is the path to genuine decentralisation.

core_ideas.explanation: Two cats fight over bread; a monkey mediates, breaking it into 'equal' halves but eating each one piece by piece, finally taking the rest as a labour fee. Pranay Kotasthane's reading: India over-debates horizontal devolution (which state gets what share) and under-debates vertical devolution (what fraction even leaves the centre). The South complains it is taxed more, but the underlying problem is that only 42% reaches states at all, and a sliver reaches cities. The monkey eats most of the bread.

The 73rd and 74th amendments treated city government and village government as one problem because they were enacted together. They aren't. A city has the minimum economies of scale to staff a public health department and run a mosquito programme; a village (~600 people) doesn't have enough civil servants, politicians, or check-and-balance for a meaningful local government. Research on village-level decentralisation is lukewarm; cities are unambiguously the right unit. The constitutional ladder should have been union list, state list, city list — and a finance commission with first-class status for cities.

core_ideas.concept: GST as the Lever of City Finance
core_ideas.explanation: GST is novel because every transaction is unambiguously attributable to a location — the shop where it took place, in a city. Kelkar, Modi and Shah envisaged splitting GST into union and state slices (5+5). It could equally be sliced 3-2-5 — three for the union, two for the state, five for the city. This bypasses the politically unfair finance-commission gauntlet that cities currently endure (sitting as supplicants at the end of two layers). Property tax has revenue limits; a GST slice for cities is the necessary structural fix.

core_ideas.concept: Migration as Meritocratic Sorting (Hirschman + James C. Scott)
core_ideas.explanation: American federalism leans on Hirschman's 'exit': if you don't like your city or state, move. James C. Scott points out early states competed for people, not territory — people are what matters, not square kilometres. From this view, India's vast migration flows are something to celebrate: people are voting with their feet for better governments. Slum life in cities is better than village life or no one would migrate. Migration sorts people by preference (progressive vs conservative places) and rewards good governments with tax revenue if the fiscal architecture lets it. Bemoaning migration is a luxury belief.
core_ideas.quote: Ultimately what matters is people, not territory.

core_ideas.concept: The Power-Accountability Mismatch in Indian Cities
core_ideas.explanation: Shruti Rajagopalan's diagnosis: in any Indian city, the people you can vote against (municipal officials) can't actually do much, and the people who can do things (state-level officials) aren't accountable to you because their vote bank is elsewhere. The lever residents pull is disconnected from the thing that moves. No amount of civic engagement fixes this; only structural realignment of authority and accountability can.

core_ideas.concept: A Choice Between Bad and Bad
core_ideas.explanation: The romantic case for decentralisation collides with reality at the sub-national level. Indian chief ministers are effectively dictators — extreme power, weak legislative check (no Rajya-Sabha-equivalent for state laws), cowed state judiciary. So you choose between a distant union with civil servants who don't know the city and unaccountable frontline staff, or a sub-national tyrant with no checks. Decentralisation must therefore be paired with a state and city level political reform — dispersion of power, more checks and balances, no autocratic mayor or chief minister.
core_ideas.quote: Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. Wherever you put concentrated power, whether in a city government or a state government, it will result in trouble.

core_ideas.concept: The Republic Thesis (from In Service of the Republic)
core_ideas.explanation: The Kelkar-Shah claim: the modern theory of economic growth and development is, at heart, about dispersion of power. A republic is a place where no one person commands; where executive, legislative and judicial branches check and balance each other. If you build a sensible republic, economic growth follows. India's failures — slow growth, persistent poverty — trace back to concentration of power and an overbearing union. The same logic applies one level down: states and cities also need to be republics, not autocracies.

Ajay's structural prescription: India should have around a hundred states; many cities should themselves be states. Calcutta is so vast and complex it should be a first-class state, separate from a remainder 'West' and 'Bengal.' A state-of-Calcutta would negotiate at the finance commission as a peer — receiving GST slices and fiscal transfers directly. This works within the existing constitutional scheme, avoiding fraught amendments. Drafting capabilities are poor today, the constituent-assembly genius is gone, so incremental refashioning is safer than a big amendment.

core_ideas.concept: Each Government Needs a Commensurate Intellectual Community
core_ideas.explanation: No government anywhere works well without a surrounding ecosystem of data, thinkers, research papers, public debate, and criticism. Decentralising power without decentralising knowledge just leaves states and cities as pure raw-power projects. Janagraha argues India has 63 groups of homogeneous cities — Bombay/Navi-Mumbai/Thane is one such group — and each group needs shared data, researchers, research organisations, and shared services. Decentralisation of decision-making must be matched by decentralisation of intelligence.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on writing his old column: 'I think that column had the headline, we should celebrate rising divorce rates.' His logic — rising divorce rates mean more women have agency to walk away from bad marriages. The provocative inversion of a moral panic.
Ajay deadpan on the Netherlands and Germany: 'Okay fine, we forgive you, you know, we know you invaded us a couple of times, but we let it go.'
Amit on the title for an imagined heavy metal album: 'Mosquitoes in Ladakh would be an incredible title for a heavy metal album.'
Amit, on Ajay's tank-themed thumbnail: 'I have a vision of a thumbnail now and the thumbnail has Ajay Shah looking out of a tank with the headline beside.'

Vasant Dhar's friend Baba claims to know everyone in the world. After Trump and Biden recognise him, Vasant insists he can't know the Pope. They go to the Vatican; the Pope appears on the balcony with Baba beside him. The man next to Vasant taps him: 'Excuse me, who's that guy with Baba?'
Ajay's tribute to states: 'When T20 cricket became popular, people said test cricket rahega, T20 rahega, we don't need ODIs anymore. So I think states are kind of like ODIs.'
Amit, mock-thanking Ajay for assuming his ignorance: when Ajay said 'mobile phone' he picked up his mobile phone to show what one looks like — 'I feel so good that I have gained new knowledge today.'

A bee buzzes around Amit's head mid-recording: 'This bee was buzzing around my head, it seems to have fallen in love with me, and while my charms are undoubted I would not welcome this particular attention.' Ajay then recites the line from R.E.M.'s 'Beat a Drum' — 'Dragonflies are busy buzzing me' — closing the loop with the show's first-episode title.

Susan Thomas's self-incriminating dog story: bitten by the family dog, she insists 'I was troubling the dog. So I mean it is fair that the dog bit me.' Ajay's gloss: 'Susan has very high standards for good behaviour.'

B.R. Ambedkar on villages: 'What is a village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow mindedness.' Cited as the cautionary case against romanticising village government — the social evils of caste and gender oppression were Ambedkar's argument for centralisation.

Kerala's COVID head start: returning Malayali students from China brought the virus back; the Kerala health system was running quarantines and isolation while the Union government had done nothing. 'We are probably three steps ahead of you in terms of figuring this thing out, don't tell us what to do.'
Albert Hirschman's Exit, Voice and Loyalty — three responses to institutional decline; American federalism leans on exit (move), India is used to loyalty or a little voice.
James C. Scott on early states: they didn't compete for territory, they competed for people — what you wanted was people to oppress.

The cartoon from Shruti Rajagopalan's lecture on constitutional amendments: a reader walks into the parliament bookshop and asks for a copy of the constitution. The bookshop replies: 'I'm sorry, we don't stock periodicals.'
The 'plagiarism test' line — Ajay's wry observation that running a plagiarism test on the Indian constitution against the Government of India Act of 1935 would catch a lot.
Lord Acton's maxim, deployed by Ajay against romantic decentralisers: 'Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.'
